items.prompt: Which keyword declares a variable in JavaScript whose binding cannot be reassigned?

options.label: let
static
const
var

rubric: `const` creates a binding that cannot be reassigned.
`let` and `var` both allow reassignment.

items.prompt: What does `typeof "hello"` return?

options.label: "char"
"string"
"object"
"text"

rubric: `typeof` on a string value returns "string".
"object" is a common mix-up with wrapper objects.

items.prompt: Which method adds an element to the end of an array?

options.label: shift()
unshift()
pop()
push()

rubric: `push()` appends to the end.
`unshift()` adds to the start; `pop()` and `shift()` remove elements.

items.prompt: Which symbol begins an arrow function's body, as in `(a, b) => a + b`?
rubric: Arrow functions use `=>`.
`->` is syntax from other languages.

items.prompt: Which keyword is used to bring a named export from another module into a file?

options.label: include
require_module
using
import

rubric: ES modules use `import`.
`include` and `using` belong to other languages.

items.prompt: Which of the following are primitive types in JavaScript? Select all that apply.

options.label: array
boolean
number
undefined

rubric: number, boolean and undefined are primitives.
Arrays are objects, not primitives.

items.prompt: A developer has an object `const user = { name: "Ana", age: 30 };` and wants to read the name using dot notation.

options.label: user[name()]
user::name
user->name
user.name

rubric: Dot notation is `user.name`.
Other options use syntax from other languages or invalid calls.

items.prompt: What is the value of `x` after `let x = 5; x += 3;`?
rubric: `+=` adds and assigns, giving 8.
53 confuses it with string concatenation.

items.prompt: Why does `console.log(typeof null)` print "object"?

options.label: null is an empty object literal
null is an instance of Object
null is converted to {} before checking
It is a long-standing quirk of the language

rubric: It is a historical quirk, not a real object.
Other options invent a conversion or inheritance.

items.prompt: What does `3 === "3"` evaluate to, and why?

options.label: false, because strings are never equal
true, because 3 is coerced to a string
false, because the types differ
true, because the values match

rubric: `===` compares without coercion, so types matter.
`==` would coerce and return true.

items.prompt: What does a variable declared with `let` inside an `if` block do after the block ends?

options.label: It becomes a global variable
It stays accessible in the whole function
It is no longer accessible
It keeps its value but is read-only

rubric: `let` is block-scoped.
Function-wide visibility is how `var` behaves.

items.prompt: What does `[1, 2, 3].map(n => n * 2)` return?

options.label: The original array changed to [2, 4, 6]
The number 12
A new array [2, 4, 6]
undefined

rubric: `map` returns a new array of transformed values.
It does not mutate the original; `forEach` returns undefined.

items.prompt: Which statements about `const` are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: A const object has frozen properties
A const variable must be declared inside a function
A const binding cannot be reassigned
A const array can still have elements pushed into it

rubric: `const` prevents rebinding but not mutation of the object.
It does not freeze properties or require a function.

items.prompt: A developer writes `class Dog { constructor(name) { this.name = name; } }` and then runs `const d = new Dog("Rex");`. They then log `d.name`.

options.label: "Rex", because the constructor stored it on the new object
"Dog", because it is the class name
undefined, because constructors cannot set properties
An error, because `this` is not available in constructors

rubric: `new` creates an object and the constructor sets `this.name`.
`this` is available in constructors.

items.prompt: What is the main difference between declaring a variable with `let` and with `const`?

options.label: `const` variables are global in scope, while `let` variables are limited to a block
`const` prevents the variable from being reassigned, while `let` allows reassignment
`const` makes the value deeply immutable, while `let` allows its contents to change
`const` variables are hoisted to the top of the file, while `let` variables are not

rubric: `const` blocks reassignment of the binding only.
The deep-immutability distractor confuses binding with value; objects declared with const can still be mutated.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes what `typeof null` returns in JavaScript?

options.label: `"undefined"`, since null means no value
`"null"`, since null is its own type name
`"number"`, since null converts to 0
`"object"`, a long-standing quirk of the language

rubric: `typeof null` is `"object"` historically.
Distractors assume the name matches the value or that coercion applies.

items.prompt: Why does `[1, 2, 3] === [1, 2, 3]` evaluate to `false`?

options.label: Array literals are always converted to strings before comparing
Arrays can only be compared with `==`, not with `===`
The two arrays hold numbers, which `===` cannot compare
Arrays are objects, and `===` compares references, not contents

rubric: Objects are compared by reference; two literals create two objects.
Distractors invent restrictions on === or assume string conversion.

items.prompt: What does an arrow function like `() => this.name` do differently from a regular function with respect to `this`?

options.label: It uses the `this` of the surrounding scope where it was defined
It leaves `this` undefined, so accessing it always throws an error
It always sets `this` to the global object when it is called
It sets `this` to the object it is called on as a method

rubric: Arrow functions capture `this` lexically.
Distractors describe regular function call-site binding or strict-mode defaults.

items.prompt: What does `Array.prototype.map` return when called on an array?

options.label: The same array, changed in place by the callback
A new array with the callback result for each element
A single value combined from all elements
The first element for which the callback returns true

rubric: map builds a new array of transformed values.
Distractors describe in-place mutation, reduce, and find.

items.prompt: Which of the following are falsy values in JavaScript? Select all that apply.

options.label: `""` (empty string)
`"0"` (string containing zero)
`NaN`
`[]` (empty array)

rubric: 0, empty string and NaN are falsy.
Non-empty strings like "0" and all arrays/objects are truthy.

items.prompt: A learner writes `const user = { name: "Ana" };` and later runs `user.name = "Bea";`. The code works without error. Then they run `user = { name: "Cy" };` and get a TypeError. Which explanation fits both results?

options.label: `const` locks property values, but reassigning a whole object is a syntax mistake
`const` makes objects editable only once, and the second change was a second edit
`const` applies only to numbers and strings, so objects behave unpredictably
`const` fixes the binding to one object, but that object's properties can still change

rubric: The binding is constant; the object is mutable.
Distractors invent edit counts or type-based behaviour.

items.prompt:
What does this code log?
`const a = [1, 2, 3, 4]; console.log(a.filter(n => n % 2 === 0).map(n => n * 10));`
rubric: filter keeps 2 and 4, then map multiplies them by 10.
[2, 4] skips the map; [10, 30] keeps odds.

items.prompt:
What does this code log?
`for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); }`
rubric: var is function scoped, so all callbacks share i, which is 3 after the loop.
0 1 2 would result from let.

items.prompt: Given `const { a, b = 5 } = { a: 1 };`, what are the values of `a` and `b`?

options.label: `a` is 1 and `b` is null
`a` is 1 and `b` is undefined
`a` is 1 and `b` is 5
`a` is undefined and `b` is 5

rubric: Default applies when the property is missing.
Other options ignore the default or misassign values.

items.prompt: You want the sum of `[3, 4, 5]`. Which call returns 12?

options.label: `[3, 4, 5].forEach((sum, n) => sum + n)`
`[3, 4, 5].reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0)`
`[3, 4, 5].filter((sum, n) => sum + n)`

rubric: reduce accumulates a single value.
map returns an array, filter an array, forEach undefined.

items.prompt: A module `math.js` contains `export function add(a, b) { return a + b; }` with no default export. Which line correctly imports and uses it in another file?

options.label: `import add from "./math.js";`
`import * as add() from "./math.js";`
`const add = export("./math.js");`
`import { add } from "./math.js";`

rubric: Named exports are imported with braces.
A default import would be undefined/error since there is no default export.

items.prompt: Which of these lines create a new array `[1, 2, 3, 4]` without modifying the original `const a = [1, 2, 3];`? Select all that apply.

options.label: `a.push(4)`
`a.slice().concat([4])`
`a.concat(4)`

rubric: Spread, concat and slice each return new arrays.
push mutates the original and returns the new length.

items.prompt: A page has `<button id="save">Save</button>`. You want clicking it to log `"saved"`. Your script runs in the page after the button element. Which code does this?

options.label: `document.querySelector("save").addEventListener("click", () => console.log("saved"));`
`document.getElementById("save").addEventListener("click", console.log("saved"));`
`document.getElementById("save").addEventListener("click", () => console.log("saved"));`
`document.getElementById("#save").onclick = "console.log('saved')";`

rubric: A function reference is passed to addEventListener.
Other options call the function immediately, use a string handler, or have wrong selectors.

items.prompt:
What does this code log?

`const fns = []; for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { fns.push(() => i * 2); } console.log(fns.map(f => f()));`
rubric: `var` gives one shared `i`, which is 3 when the closures run, so each returns 6.
[0, 2, 4] assumes each iteration has its own `i`, as `let` would give.

items.prompt:
What do `b` and `rest` hold after this runs?

`const { a, b = 5, ...rest } = { a: 1, b: undefined, c: 3, d: 4 };`

options.label: undefined and { c: 3, d: 4 }
5 and { b: undefined, c: 3, d: 4 }

rubric: A default applies when the value is undefined, and object rest collects the remaining keys except a and b.
Distractors assume the default is skipped, rest produces an array, or b stays in rest.

items.prompt:
What does this expression evaluate to?

`[1, 2, 3, 4].reduce((acc, n) => (n % 2 ? acc : acc + n), 10)`
rubric: The accumulator starts at 10 and only the even numbers 2 and 4 are added, giving 16.
6 ignores the initial value; 10 and 20 misread the parity test.

items.prompt: Given `const counter = { n: 0, inc() { this.n++; } };`, which snippet leaves `counter.n` equal to 1 when run in a module?

options.label: `const f = counter.inc; f.call();`
`const f = counter.inc; f();`
`const f = counter.inc.bind(null); f();`
`const f = counter.inc.bind(counter); f();`

rubric: `bind(counter)` fixes `this` to the object, so the method increments `counter.n`.
The other snippets call the detached method with `this` undefined or null, so they throw or miss the object.

items.prompt:
In what order are the letters logged?

`console.log('A'); setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C')); console.log('D');`

options.label: A C D B
A D C B
A D B C
A B C D

rubric: Synchronous logs run first (A, D), then the promise microtask (C), then the timer callback (B).
A D B C puts the timer before the microtask, a common event loop misconception.

items.prompt: Given `const arr = [1, 2, 3];`, which expressions leave `arr` itself unchanged? Select all that apply.

options.label: `arr.concat([4])`
`arr.splice(0, 1)`
`arr.push(4)`
`arr.filter(x => x > 1)`

rubric: `concat` and `filter` return new arrays without touching the original.
`splice` and `push` mutate the array in place.

items.prompt: A file `utils.js` contains `export function fmt(n) { ... }` and `export default function parse(s) { ... }`. In `main.js` you need to call both `parse` and `fmt`. Which import statement does this correctly?

options.label: `import { parse, fmt } from './utils.js';`
`import parse, { fmt } from './utils.js';`
`import * as parse from './utils.js'; parse('1');`
`import { default as fmt, parse } from './utils.js';`

rubric: The default export is imported without braces and named exports go inside braces.
Distractors treat the default export as a named one, swap the bindings, or call a namespace object as a function.

items.prompt: After `const user = { name: 'a', tags: ['x'] }; const copy = { ...user }; copy.tags.push('y');`, `user.tags` is `['x', 'y']`. What explains this?

options.label: `push` always changes a prototype that every object spread from `user` shares
Spread makes a shallow copy, so `copy.tags` and `user.tags` point to the same array object
Objects declared with `const` share their nested arrays with any object spread from them
Spread copies by reference only when the array is non-empty, so tags stayed linked

rubric: Spread copies top-level properties only, so nested objects and arrays are shared by reference.
Distractors invent rules about emptiness, prototypes or `const`.

items.prompt: `items.forEach(async id => { await save(id); }); console.log('done');` logs 'done' before the saves finish. What is the cause?

options.label: `forEach` runs its callbacks on a separate thread, so 'done' can log while saves are running
`forEach` ignores the promises returned by its async callback, so it does not wait for any save
`save` must return a callback rather than a promise, otherwise `await` resumes immediately
`await` inside an arrow function is skipped unless the arrow function is wrapped in parentheses

rubric: `forEach` discards callback return values, so nothing awaits the promises; use `for...of` or `Promise.all` with `map`.
Distractors blame threads, parentheses or the return type of `save`.

items.prompt: `class B extends A { constructor() { this.x = 1; super(); } }` throws when `new B()` runs. What is the cause?

options.label: Class fields must be declared before a constructor can assign `this.x`
Derived classes cannot define their own constructor unless the base class has none
`super()` must receive the value of `this.x` as an argument to initialise it
`this` cannot be used in a derived constructor before `super()` has run, so a ReferenceError is thrown

rubric: In a derived class, `this` is uninitialised until `super()` returns.
Distractors invent field-declaration or constructor restrictions.

items.prompt: `const DEFAULT = []; function add(x, list = DEFAULT) { list.push(x); return list; }` returns `[1, 2]` on the second call `add(2)` after `add(1)`. Why?

options.label: Default parameter values are evaluated once at definition, so every call reuses one array
`DEFAULT` is a shared array that every call without `list` receives, so pushes accumulate
Default parameters are evaluated per call, but `const` arrays cannot be reassigned, so push appends twice
`push` copies the array on each call, so earlier results are lost and later ones kept

rubric: The default expression is evaluated per call but yields the same shared array object each time.
The first distractor misstates when defaults are evaluated; the others misdescribe `push` and `const`.

items.prompt: `async function load() { try { return fetchData(); } catch (e) { return fallback; } }` never returns `fallback` when `fetchData()` rejects. Why?

options.label: Async functions wrap every returned value in a new promise, which swallows the rejection before catch runs
`return` without `await` hands back the promise, so the rejection happens after the try block has exited and skips the catch
`catch` only handles errors thrown by `await` expressions on promises that were already resolved earlier
`try` blocks inside async functions run on a later microtask, so the catch is registered too late

rubric: Without `await` the try block finishes before the promise settles, so the catch cannot see the rejection; use `return await`.
Distractors give false rules about wrapping and microtask timing.

items.prompt: Each snippet below is run on its own in a module. Which ones throw a ReferenceError? Select all that apply.

options.label: `console.log(b); let b = 2;`
`console.log(typeof d); let d = 3;`
`console.log(typeof c);` where `c` is never declared
`console.log(a); var a = 1;`

rubric: Reading a `let` variable in its temporal dead zone throws, even through `typeof`.
`var` is hoisted as undefined, and `typeof` on an undeclared name is safe.

items.prompt: Your app's entry file `a.js` imports `b.js`, and `b.js` also imports `a.js`. `a.js` has `export const config = { debug: true };` after its imports. `b.js` reads `config.debug` at its top level and the app crashes on startup. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Named exports are copied into `b.js` when imported, so the copy was made before `config` existed
`b.js` evaluates before `a.js` finishes, so `config` is still in its temporal dead zone
`config` is exported with `const`, which makes it unreadable by any other module
ES modules forbid circular imports, so the loader rejects the second import of `a.js`

rubric: Circular imports are allowed, but `b.js` runs first and reads `config` before its declaration has executed, causing a ReferenceError.
Distractors claim cycles are forbidden, that `const` blocks sharing, or that imports are copies rather than live bindings.

items.prompt: What does `fns.map(f => f())` return after `const fns = []; for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { fns.push(() => i); i++; }` runs?
rubric: Each iteration gets its own copy of `i`; the body's `i++` changes that copy before the next iteration copies it, so the closures see 1 and 3.
[0, 2] ignores the increment inside the body; [3, 3] applies the `var` model.

items.prompt: Given `class Counter { count = 0; inc() { this.count++; } } const c = new Counter(); const { inc } = c; inc();`, what happens on the last line?

options.label: `c.count` becomes 1, because the destructured `inc` keeps its binding to `c`
A global `count` is created, because non-strict `this` falls back to the global object
A TypeError, because `this` is undefined in a strict-mode class method called unbound
`NaN` is stored on `c`, because `this.count` is read from the prototype

rubric: Class bodies are strict, and a detached method call gets `this` as undefined, so `this.count` throws a TypeError.
Distractors assume sloppy-mode globals or that methods are auto-bound.

items.prompt: What is logged? `console.log('A'); setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C')).then(() => console.log('D')); (async () => { console.log('E'); await null; console.log('F'); })(); console.log('G');`

options.label: A E G C F D B
A E G C D F B
A G E C D F B
A E G B C D F

rubric: Sync code logs A, E, G. The microtask queue holds C then F; C queues D after F, so the order is C F D, and the timer B runs last.
A E G C D F B wrongly assumes the chained `then` runs before the async continuation.

items.prompt: `a.js` is the entry point: `import { helper } from './b.js'; export const value = 42;`. `b.js` contains: `import { value } from './a.js'; export const helper = value * 2;`. What happens when `a.js` runs as an ES module?

options.label: The import cycle is rejected with a SyntaxError before any code runs
`b.js` throws a ReferenceError, because `value` is still uninitialised when `b.js` evaluates
`helper` is 84, because imports are hoisted and `value` is already assigned
`helper` is NaN, because `value` is undefined during the cycle

rubric: `b.js` evaluates first and reads `value` while it is still in its temporal dead zone, so it throws a ReferenceError.
`helper` being NaN is the `var`/CommonJS partial-export intuition.

items.prompt: `try { items.forEach(async (item) => { await save(item); }); } catch (e) { report(e); }` If `save` rejects for one item, why is `report` never called?

options.label: `await` inside a callback converts a rejection into a resolved `undefined` value
`catch` only handles errors thrown by built-in methods, never by user-defined functions
`forEach` discards the promises the callbacks return, so rejections escape the `try` block unhandled
`forEach` runs its callbacks on separate threads, so `catch` executes on another thread

rubric: `forEach` ignores callback return values, so the rejected promises are never awaited inside the `try`.
The thread and built-in explanations misread how async errors propagate.

items.prompt: With `const cfg = { a: 1, nested: { b: 2 } }; const copy = { ...cfg };`, which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: After `copy.nested.b = 5`, `cfg.nested.b` is also 5
After `copy.a = 9`, `cfg.a` is also 9
After `copy.nested = { b: 7 }`, `cfg.nested.b` is still 2
Spread copies `nested` deeply, so `cfg.nested.b` stays 2 after `copy.nested.b = 5`

rubric: Spread is a shallow copy: nested objects are shared, but reassigning a property on the copy does not affect the original.
Distractors claim primitives are shared or that spread clones deeply.

items.prompt: A single-page app keeps a module-level `const meta = new Map()` that maps DOM elements to computed layout data. After many navigations, memory keeps growing even though old views are removed from the document. Heap snapshots show many detached DOM nodes. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The Map holds strong references to its element keys, so removed nodes can never be garbage collected
Event listeners on removed nodes are always kept alive by the browser's event loop
Map entries are copied on every lookup, so each navigation duplicates the stored data
`removeChild` only hides nodes, and the garbage collector frees them at page unload

rubric: A Map keeps its keys reachable; a WeakMap would let detached nodes be collected.
Other options misdescribe how garbage collection or removal works.

items.prompt: A dashboard loads five independent widgets from five endpoints. Criteria: one failing endpoint must not blank the others, and each widget shows its own error state. Which approach fits best?

options.label: `Promise.race`, rendering whichever widget settles first
Sequential `await` calls in a single `try` block
`Promise.allSettled`, rendering each result or its error per widget
`Promise.all`, with one `catch` that shows a page-wide error

rubric: `allSettled` reports every outcome, so each widget handles its own success or failure.
`Promise.all` rejects on the first failure, discarding the other results.

items.prompt: You must deep-copy a state object containing nested objects, `Date` values and a `Map`, with no functions inside. Criteria: types must be preserved, no dependencies, minimal code. Which option is best?

options.label: `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(state))`, because it handles every serialisable value
A recursive `Object.assign` over each key, because it copies nested values
`{ ...state }`, because spread copies every nested level
`structuredClone(state)`, because it preserves dates and maps without a library

rubric: `structuredClone` keeps Date and Map types; JSON turns Dates into strings and Maps into empty objects.
Spread and `Object.assign` are shallow.

items.prompt: You need a class with thousands of instances, hard privacy of internal state, and low per-instance memory. Which design best meets all three criteria?

options.label: A factory function returning an object whose methods close over local variables
A class storing state under `Symbol` keys and methods on the prototype
A class with `_state` fields and a documented rule not to touch them
A class using `#private` fields with methods defined once on the prototype

rubric: `#private` fields are enforced by the language, and prototype methods are shared across instances.
Closure factories create per-instance functions; `_` is only a convention; Symbols are discoverable via reflection.

items.prompt: `createChart(el, true, false, 3, null, true)` is widely used. Criteria: readable call sites, and new options can be added later without breaking existing callers. Which redesign is best?

options.label: Read the options from a shared module-level config object that callers mutate
Split it into six functions, one per boolean combination, to make intent clear
Keep positional parameters and append each new option at the end with a default
Accept `(el, { animate = true, legend = false, ... } = {})` as a single options object

rubric: A destructured options object names each argument and lets options be added without changing the call signature.
Appended positional parameters stay unreadable; a mutable global creates hidden coupling.

items.prompt: A 300 KB charting library is used only on an admin page visited by about 2% of users. Criteria: keep first load fast for everyone, and a brief delay when opening the admin page is acceptable. Which approach is best?

options.label: Load it with `import('./charts.js')` when the admin page opens
Add a static `import` at the top of the main entry file
Inline the library in the HTML so there is no extra request
Load it in a blocking script in the page head for all users

rubric: Dynamic `import()` defers the cost to the few users who need it.
Static imports and head scripts add the cost to every first load.

items.prompt: A cache is keyed by user-supplied strings. Which are sound reasons to prefer a `Map` over a plain object `{}` for it? Select all that apply.

options.label: Entries are removed automatically once the key is no longer referenced elsewhere
Lookups are always faster than property access, whatever the data size
Keys like `constructor` or `__proto__` cannot collide with inherited properties
The `size` property gives the entry count directly without counting keys

rubric: A Map avoids prototype-key collisions and exposes `size` directly.
Automatic key collection describes WeakMap, and the speed claim is not guaranteed.

items.prompt: A Node service runs `records.filter(isValid).map(normalise).filter(isRecent)` on about 2 million records, and peak memory spikes from the intermediate arrays. Criteria: lower peak memory, no new dependencies, and each step stays a separate named function. Which change fits best?

options.label: Rewrite each step as `forEach` that pushes into outer arrays
Call `global.gc()` between the chained steps to free each intermediate array
Make each step a generator and consume the chain lazily with `for...of`
Wrap each step in `Promise.all` so the steps run in parallel

rubric: Chained generators process one record at a time, so no full intermediate arrays are held and steps stay named.
`forEach` with outer arrays and manual GC still hold the full data, and parallel promises do not reduce memory.

items.prompt: A service must snapshot a state object holding `Date` values, a `Map`, and keys whose value is `undefined`. It has no functions or class instances. Judged on fidelity of the copy with the least custom code, which approach is best?

options.label: `{ ...state }`, because spread recursively copies nested objects and collections
`JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(state))`, because it deep-copies every value type faithfully
`Object.assign({}, state)`, because it clones Dates and Maps into independent copies
`structuredClone(state)`, because it keeps Dates and Maps as real Dates and Maps

rubric: structuredClone supports Date and Map and preserves undefined values, so it fits the criteria.
JSON turns Dates into strings, empties Maps and drops undefined keys; spread and assign are shallow.

items.prompt: A reviewer claims: `const config = Object.freeze({ db: { host: 'a' }, retries: 3 })` guarantees config can never change. Which critique of the claim is correct?

options.label: Freeze is shallow, so `config.db.host` can still be reassigned unless nested objects are frozen too
Freeze is deep but only in strict mode, so non-strict code can mutate nested values
Freeze works only inside classes, so a plain object literal remains fully mutable
Freeze only blocks deleting properties, so `config.retries = 5` still succeeds in all modes

rubric: Object.freeze affects only the object's own properties, not the objects they reference.
Distractors misstate freeze as deep, partial or class-limited.

items.prompt: You store computed layout metadata per DOM element in a long-lived module. Elements are removed from the page often. Criteria: metadata must not keep removed elements in memory, and you never need to iterate the entries. Which structure is best?

options.label: A `Map` keyed by element, deleting entries manually whenever any code path removes an element
A plain object keyed by `element.id`, since string keys are garbage collected automatically
An array of `[element, data]` pairs, since arrays release unreferenced items on each GC cycle
A `WeakMap` keyed by element, so entries become collectible once the element is unreachable

rubric: WeakMap holds keys weakly and needs no iteration here, matching both criteria.
Map and arrays retain strong references; manual cleanup is fragile and id-keyed objects never free themselves.

items.prompt: A table renders 10,000 rows and adds or removes rows constantly. Each row has a click action. Criteria: low memory, no re-binding after DOM updates. Which is the best judgement, and its main caveat?

options.label: Bind a listener on every row, because each handler is isolated and the added memory is negligible
Bind a listener on every row and rebind after each render, because bubbling is unreliable for clicks
Use one delegated listener on the table body, noting it fails for events that do not bubble
Use one delegated listener on `document`, because events never need to bubble to reach it

rubric: Delegation uses one handler that works for rows added later; the caveat is non-bubbling events such as focus or blur.
Per-row binding costs memory and rebinding; the last option misstates how bubbling works.

items.prompt: A dashboard loads five independent widgets from separate endpoints. Criteria: show every widget that succeeded, display an error only in widgets that failed, and never blank the whole page. Which approach is best?

options.label: `Promise.any(requests)`, since it collects each fulfilled value and reports every rejection
`Promise.race(requests)`, since the first settled promise gives the fastest overall render
`Promise.allSettled(requests)`, then render each fulfilled value and show errors for rejected ones
`Promise.all(requests)` in a try/catch, since one catch handles every individual failure

rubric: allSettled reports each outcome so partial success is rendered.
Promise.all rejects on first failure, race and any return only a single result.

items.prompt: A reviewer examines `items.forEach(async (x) => { await save(x); }); console.log('done');` inside a try/catch. Which criticisms are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: `await Promise.all(items.map(save))` fixes both problems and keeps the saves concurrent
`forEach` ignores the returned promises, so 'done' logs before saves finish
The `await` makes the saves run strictly one after another, so ordering is guaranteed
A rejected `save` cannot be caught by the surrounding try/catch and surfaces as unhandled
Marking the callback `async` makes `forEach` pause until each callback has resolved

rubric: forEach discards promises, so completion and errors escape the caller; Promise.all over map restores both.
The sequencing and async-forEach-waits claims misread how forEach and await interact.

items.prompt: You maintain a library whose `Client` class holds an API token. Thousands of instances are created, subclasses must exist, and consumers must not read the token. Tests need no access to it. Which implementation best meets these criteria?

options.label: A factory closure per instance defining every method inside it, so subclassing via `extends` still works naturally
Underscore-named property `_token`, since the convention reliably prevents outside reads
A `#token` private field with shared prototype methods, so privacy is enforced and methods are not duplicated
A module-level `Symbol` key stored as a property, since symbol properties are hidden from every API

rubric: Private fields are truly inaccessible and keep methods on the shared prototype, supporting subclassing.
Underscores are convention only, per-instance closures duplicate methods and break extends, and symbols are discoverable via getOwnPropertySymbols.

items.prompt: Design a `debounce(fn, ms)` that must preserve the caller's `this`, call `fn` with the latest arguments only, and expose `cancel()`. Which design meets every constraint?

options.label: Return an arrow function that clears and resets the timer calling `fn(...args)`; `cancel` clears the timer
Return a regular function that sets a timer without clearing the old one, calling `fn.apply(this, args)`; `cancel` clears the last
Return a regular function that clears the timer, then sets one calling `fn.apply(this, args)`; `cancel` clears the timer
Return a regular function that clears and resets the timer using the first call's args via `fn.apply(this, first)`; `cancel` clears it

rubric: A regular function keeps the call-site this, clearing resets the delay, and the latest args are used.
Arrow loses this, no clearing fires every call, and first-call args violate the latest-args rule.

items.prompt: A search box fires `fetch` per keystroke. Constraints: only the latest query's results may render, and superseded requests must stop consuming bandwidth. Which design meets both?

options.label: Disable the input while a request is pending, so overlapping requests cannot happen at all
Abort the previous `AbortController` before each new fetch, passing `signal`, and ignore `AbortError` rejections
Debounce input at 50 ms and render whichever response arrives first, as it must be the freshest
Keep a request counter and ignore stale responses, letting every older request run to completion

rubric: Aborting cancels the old network work and guarantees stale responses never render.
A counter ignores stale data but still uses bandwidth; first-arrival is not ordered; disabling input breaks typing.

items.prompt: Design a `range(1, 4)` result that is lazy and can be looped with `for...of` multiple times, each loop restarting from 1. Which design meets this?

options.label: Return the object produced by calling a generator function once, and reuse it for every loop
Return an object whose `[Symbol.iterator]` is a generator method, so each loop gets a fresh generator
Return an iterator object with only a `next()` method that resets itself after reaching the end
Return an array built eagerly with a loop, since arrays are lazily iterated by `for...of`

rubric: An iterable producing a new iterator per loop is lazy and re-iterable.
A single generator object is exhausted after one loop, arrays are eager, and a bare iterator is not iterable.

items.prompt: ES modules `a.js` and `b.js` import each other, and `a.js` calls a function from `b.js` at its top level, causing a ReferenceError for an uninitialised binding. Which redesign removes the cycle while keeping both modules' behaviour?

options.label: Swap the import order in `a.js` so `b.js` is declared before its own dependencies
Move the shared logic to a third module `c.js` that both `a.js` and `b.js` import
Change both imports to dynamic `import()` calls at the top level without `await`
Rename the exports in `b.js` to `var` declarations so hoisting makes them available

rubric: Extracting shared code to a third module breaks the cycle so no module reads an uninitialised binding.
Reordering, un-awaited dynamic imports, or var do not fix evaluation order in a cycle.

items.prompt: Design `memoize(fn)` for a function taking exactly one object argument. Constraints: results are cached per object identity, and cached entries must not keep otherwise unreachable objects alive. Which design fits?

options.label: A `WeakMap` from the argument object to its computed result, checked before calling `fn`
A `Map` keyed by the object, clearing it on a timer, since a Map holds keys only weakly
An object keyed by `JSON.stringify(arg)`, since equal content then shares one identity
An array of recent `[arg, result]` pairs, trimmed periodically so memory use stays bounded

rubric: WeakMap keys by identity and does not prevent collection of the key objects.
Map holds keys strongly, JSON keys ignore identity, and an array retains objects until trimmed.

items.prompt: Design an event emitter with these requirements: a handler removing itself during `emit` must not cause others to be skipped, one throwing handler must not stop the rest, and callers can unsubscribe without keeping the handler reference. Which elements are needed? Select all that apply.

options.label: Sort the handler list on each `emit` so removals are applied first
Wrap each handler call in try/catch and report errors after the loop
Iterate over a copy of the handler list during `emit`
Loop over the handlers with `for...in` so removal is handled automatically
Have `on` return an unsubscribe function that removes that handler

rubric: A copy protects iteration, try/catch isolates failures, and a returned unsubscribe meets the no-reference need.
for...in and sorting do not address mutation during emit, errors, or unsubscription.

items.prompt: You must run 100 async upload tasks with at most 3 in flight at once. Slow tasks must not leave slots idle, and the results array must match input order. Which design meets every constraint?

options.label: Split tasks into groups of three and `await Promise.all` each group before starting the next group
Run tasks one after another in a `for...of` with `await`, which keeps ordering and never exceeds three
Call `Promise.all(tasks.map(t => t()))` so the runtime limits concurrency to three internally
Start three workers that each loop, taking the next shared index and storing `results[i]`, then await all workers

rubric: Workers pulling a shared index keep three slots busy and write results by index to preserve order.
Batching idles slots behind the slowest task, Promise.all starts all 100, and sequential runs one at a time.
